title: Two Flights, Three Hundred Times a Year. The Case of the Stairwell
body: My building has five floors and an elevator that smells faintly of other people's dinners. Two years ago I decided, without ceremony, to stop taking it when going up two flights or less from the ground floor. No tracker, no challenge group, no before photos. Just a rule and a door that says STAIRS. This is the full accounting of what that small rule bought, written down because nobody believes small things anymore without a ledger. The raw arithmetic. I enter my building about twice a day on ordinary days, call it six hundred ascents a year, and under the rule roughly five hundred of those now happen on foot, two flights each, ten steps a flight, so about ten thousand stairs a year, which sounds dramatic and feels like nothing, which is exactly the point. Each climb takes me twenty to twenty-five seconds. The elevator, door to door, takes about forty once you count the wait, because elevators are a lottery you enter every time. The stairs are faster at this height and I have timed both, twice, on different weeks, because I am the kind of person who will eventually time it. The body's response was quiet and cumulative. I did not lose weight; I never expected a staircase to fight a bakery, and honesty laws apply to stairwells too. What changed. My knees stopped announcing the first flight of every hike. My resting pace up steep streets improved by one notch of the scale I keep in my head. Somewhere around month eight I noticed I no longer do the little negotiation at the building door, the two-second debate between comfort and the rule, because the rule became the default and defaults do not negotiate. That, more than the legs, is the dividend. A decision removed from daily life is worth more than a decision made well. The elevator, relieved of my two-flight errands, still serves its true constituents. The neighbor from the fourth floor with the double stroller, the man with the delivery boxes, anyone older, anyone tired, anyone carrying anything heavier than a laptop. This is the part I want to defend. Taking the stairs when you can is not a judgment of people who take the elevator; it is what keeps the elevator available and unresented for the people for whom it is not a choice. A stairwell culture where the able-bodied opt out of the queue is quietly kinder to everyone still in it. The costs, honestly stated. In summer the stairwell is warm and I arrive at my door with the general dignity of a man who has just climbed stairs, which is fine, because the alternative is arriving cool and having climbed nothing. Twice I carried groceries up while wearing a backpack and regretted my life choices for eleven seconds. And once, in the first week, I took the elevator out of pure habit, remembered at the third floor, and laughed at myself in the mirrored wall, which the elevator offers for exactly such occasions. The transferable idea is not about stairs. It is about any two-flight-sized effort you face daily. The walk to the closer bus stop, the hand-washed pan, the one-paragraph reply done properly. Individually they are invisible. Six hundred times a year they are a person. Pick yours, write the rule in one sentence, and let the door that says STAIRS do the deciding for a year. Then keep the honest ledger, the way nobody does, and see what small bought.
